title: [2605.30352] Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time

sections.heading: Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time

content.text: Moving Object Segmentation (MOS) aims to discover, segment, and track objects that move independently of the camera. Current MOS methods, however, exhibit two fundamental limitations: they rely on pre-computed 2D auxiliary modalities such as optical flow or point trajectories that lack 3D geometric information, and they treat motion as a sequence-level attribute, overlooking the instantaneous motion state of each object. We address both by grounding MOS in 3D space and time, and propose Gmos, a framework that operates directly on RGB video to produce 3D-aware, temporally fine-grained segmentation of multiple moving objects, alongside a foreground–background variant Gmos-S for faster deployment. To support training and evaluation in this regime, we curate Gmos-2K, a dataset of 2,2102{,}210 real-world videos with per-object temporal motion annotations drawn from five established Video Object Segmentation (VOS) benchmarks, and formalise MOS-I (“I” for instantaneous), a temporally fine-grained evaluation protocol with three complementary metrics. Gmos achieves state-of-the-art results across MOS, MOS-I, and Unsupervised VOS benchmarks, while running significantly faster than prior multi-object MOS methods and supporting online inference for streaming deployment.

Moving object segmentation (MOS) aims to discover, segment, and track objects that move independently of the camera. This capability is foundational to applications such as autonomous driving [[5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib77 "Moving object segmentation in 3D LiDAR data: a learning-based approach exploiting sequential data"), [33](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib78 "Multi-sensor fusion for robust localization with moving object segmentation in complex dynamic 3D scenes")], camouflaged object detection [Lamdouar20, Yang21a], and video surveillance [[45](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib76 "Deep anomaly detection through visual attention in surveillance videos"), [65](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib79 "Attention-based temporal encoding network with background-independent motion mask for action recognition")], and has become increasingly central to recent 3D/4D scene reconstruction methods [[35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib51 "MegaSaM: accurate, fast and robust structure and motion from casual dynamic videos"), [19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib52 "RoMo: robust motion segmentation improves structure from motion")] that require motion masks to separate dynamic objects from the static scene.

Current MOS methods exhibit two fundamental limitations, as outlined in [Tab.˜1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S1.T1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time"). *First*, they are not 3D-aware and remain fragile under large camera motion or depth parallax. This stems from their heavy reliance on pre-computed 2D auxiliary modalities (e.g. optical flow [Yang21a, Xie22, [36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib59 "Bootstrapping objectness from videos by relaxed common fate and visual grouping")] or point trajectories [[22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib61 "Segment any motion in videos"), Karazija24b]), which lack 3D geometric information and incur substantial pre-processing overhead. *Second*, existing benchmarks assume that objects move throughout the video, leading methods to treat motion as a *sequence-level* attribute and to overlook the instantaneous motion state of each object. This coarse temporal granularity precludes online and real-time deployment.

We address both limitations by grounding MOS in *space* and *time*. Our approach rests on two observations: (i) the geometric representations learnt by recent feed-forward 3D reconstruction models already encode sufficient information to disentangle camera and object motion, and (ii) independent object motion is reliably identifiable from a short temporal window (∼\sim0.50.5 s).

Building on these insights, we propose Gmos, a proposer–propagator framework that operates directly on RGB video without any auxiliary pre-computed modalities. A per-frame *proposer* fuses geometric features from a π3\pi^{3} encoder [[64](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib54 "π3: Permutation-equivariant visual geometry learning")] with segmentation features from a SAM2 encoder [[55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib7 "SAM 2: segment anything in images and videos")], jointly producing object mask proposals and per-frame motion-state predictions. A SAM2-based *propagator* then links these proposals into consistent tracks across frames. We further introduce Gmos-S (“S” for *single*), a streaming foreground–background variant that predicts all moving objects as a *single binary* mask and dispenses with the propagator for even faster inference.

To support MOS in a more geometrically grounded and temporally fine-grained manner, we curate Gmos-2K, a collection of 2,2102{,}210 real-world videos drawn from five established VOS benchmarks and annotated with per-frame motion states for every object. The subsets span complementary domains, including heavily occluded scenes, hand–object interactions, and wildlife and human-centric clips. Alongside this dataset, we formalise MOS-I (“I” for *instantaneous*), a temporally fine-grained MOS evaluation protocol. As illustrated in [Fig.˜1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S0.F1 "In Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") (right), MOS-I scores segmentation masks only on frames where objects are actively moving, and penalises false-positive predictions on static and background objects.
In summary, our contributions are as follows:

* • We propose Gmos, a proposer–propagator framework that delivers 3D-aware, temporally fine-grained MOS from RGB video alone and supports online inference. We also introduce Gmos-S, a foreground–background variant for even faster deployment. * • We introduce a confidence-based training objective that automatically down-weights noisy frame-level motion annotations near static–moving transitions. * • We curate Gmos-2K, a dataset of 2,2102{,}210 real-world videos drawn from five established VOS benchmarks and annotated with per-object temporal motion labels, providing a unified resource for both training and evaluating temporally fine-grained MOS methods. * • We formalise MOS-I, a temporally fine-grained evaluation protocol for MOS, together with three complementary metrics that jointly measure segmentation accuracy on actively moving frames and robustness to false-positive predictions on static and background objects.

Gmos achieves state-of-the-art results across MOS, MOS-I, and Unsupervised VOS (UVOS) benchmarks, while running roughly three times faster than prior MOS methods ([Tab.˜1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S1.T1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time")).

Gmos produces these outputs jointly, and therefore covers both MOS-I ([Sec.˜4.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S4.SS2 "4.2 Benchmarks for evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time")) and the conventional MOS settings.

[Fig.˜2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S2.F2 "In 2.1 Gmos proposer ‣ 2 Method: Gmos ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") (left) provides an overview of Gmos, which follows a *proposer-propagator* design. The proposer operates on a short local window and outputs, for the middle frame, a set of NN per-object proposals, each comprising a moving object mask and a predicted motion state. The propagator then links these per-frame proposals into consistent object tracks across the full video.

As illustrated in [Fig.˜2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S2.F2 "In 2.1 Gmos proposer ‣ 2 Method: Gmos ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") (right), the proposer takes raw video frames as its sole input and predicts, for each of NN object queries, a segmentation mask together with auxiliary outputs: a confidence score, a motion state, and an estimated mask IoU.

Geometric encoder. To achieve *3D-awareness*, we extract geometric features using a frozen π3\pi^{3} encoder [[64](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib54 "π3: Permutation-equivariant visual geometry learning")]. Rather than feeding the entire sequence, we process a short temporal window [t−n,t+n][t-n,\,t+n] centred at the query frame tt, sufficient for distinguishing independent object motion from camera-induced parallax. After π3\pi^{3} encoding, we retain only the *middle-frame* feature ftgeo∈ℝhg×wg×dgf^{\text{geo}}\_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\_{\text{g}}\times w\_{\text{g}}\times d\_{\text{g}}}, as inter-frame correspondence is already encoded in it through the model’s cross-frame attention.

Segmentation encoder. Since geometric features alone encode little about object segmentation cues, we leverage the strong objectness prior of a frozen SAM2 encoder [[55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib7 "SAM 2: segment anything in images and videos")]. Only the query frame ItI\_{t} is passed through SAM2, yielding a bottleneck feature ftseg∈ℝh×w×df^{\text{seg}}\_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times w\times d} together with high-resolution features that are later used by the mask head.

Feature fusion. The geometric feature ftgeof^{\text{geo}}\_{t} is typically at a lower spatial resolution than the segmentation one ftsegf^{\text{seg}}\_{t}, i.e. hg<hh\_{\text{g}}<h. We therefore bilinearly interpolate ftgeof^{\text{geo}}\_{t} to (h,w)(h,w), concatenate the two features channel-wise, and apply a linear projection to obtain the fused feature ft∈ℝh×w×df\_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times w\times d}. A light-weight transformer self-attention encoder is then applied to ftf\_{t} to enforce global spatial consistency.

Transformer decoder. Following the convention in query-based segmentation [[7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib74 "Per-pixel classification is not all you need for semantic segmentation"), [31](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib75 "Mask dino: towards a unified transformer-based framework for object detection and segmentation")], we introduce NN learnable object queries {q(i)}i=1N\{q^{(i)}\}\_{i=1}^{N} with q(i)∈ℝdq^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and feed them into a two-way transformer decoder [[27](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib19 "Segment anything")] together with ftf\_{t}. Each layer alternates query self-attention with query-to-feature and feature-to-query cross-attention, producing refined query tokens {qt∗(i)}\{q^{\*(i)}\_{t}\} and refined dense features ft∗∈ℝh×w×df^{\*}\_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times w\times d}.

Mask head. The refined dense features ft∗{f}^{\*}\_{t} are upsampled to full resolution through transposed convolutions, with the SAM2 high-resolution features added as skip connections. An MLP maps each refined query qt∗(i){q}^{\*(i)}\_{t} to a mask embedding, and the per-query mask M^t(i)\hat{M}^{(i)}\_{t} is obtained by dot product with the upsampled features, following the hypernetwork design in [[7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib74 "Per-pixel classification is not all you need for semantic segmentation")]. During training, queries are matched to ground truth via bipartite Hungarian assignment. Note, an object’s ground-truth mask is defined as *empty* whenever the object is not moving, so supervision jointly shapes the mask and the motion state.

Motion and IoU heads. Two independent MLP heads take in the refined query qt∗(i){q}^{\*(i)}\_{t}. The *motion head* leads to the probability m^t(i)\hat{m}^{(i)}\_{t} that object ii is moving at frame tt, and the *IoU head* produces a scalar u^t(i)\hat{u}^{(i)}\_{t} estimating the quality of M^t(i)\hat{M}^{(i)}\_{t} in terms of its expected IoU against the ground truth.

Confidence prediction. The instantaneous motion state is inherently ambiguous near transitions between motion and rest, where the ground truth switches abruptly between a full mask with mt(i)=1m^{(i)}\_{t}=1 and an empty mask with mt(i)=0m^{(i)}\_{t}=0. To mitigate this label noise, we follow [[62](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib48 "DUSt3R: geometric 3d vision made easy")] and introduce a learnable per-query confidence c^t(i)∈[0,1]\hat{c}^{(i)}\_{t}\in[0,1], predicted by a final MLP head with sigmoid output. The resulting confidence modulates the mask and motion losses (see [Eq.˜2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S2.E2 "In 2.1 Gmos proposer ‣ 2 Method: Gmos ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time")).
Training objective. The total proposer loss reads

The loss is averaged over object queries ii and frames tt, with the corresponding indices dropped for clarity. Here, ℒmask\mathcal{L}\_{\text{mask}} is a mixture of focal and dice losses, ℒmotion\mathcal{L}\_{\text{motion}} is a binary cross-entropy on the motion state, and ℒiou\mathcal{L}\_{\text{iou}} is an MSE loss between the predicted IoU and the actual IoU against the ground truth.

The mask and motion losses are modulated by a rescaled confidence c~=(cmax−1)​c^+1∈[1,cmax]\tilde{c}=(c\_{\max}-1)\,\hat{c}+1\in[1,c\_{\max}], and the last term is an adversarial confidence regulariser [[62](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib48 "DUSt3R: geometric 3d vision made easy")] that raises c~\tilde{c} on clean, easy samples the model can solve precisely. For difficult examples, such as a walking pedestrian coming to a stop, the mask and motion losses are large due to label ambiguity around the transition. The model therefore lowers c~\tilde{c} to attenuate the multiplicative term, paying a small log⁡c~\log\tilde{c} penalty in exchange.

In practice, the confidence would be driven up only for static samples, since predicting an empty mask for a static object is trivially easier than predicting a precise moving-object mask, failing to address the transition noise. We therefore *split* the regularisation by the ground-truth motion state mm, using distinct coefficients λconfmov\lambda^{\text{mov}}\_{\text{conf}} and λconfsta\lambda^{\text{sta}}\_{\text{conf}} to calibrate moving and static samples independently.

Gmos-S: a foreground–background variant. For efficiency-critical deployment, we additionally instantiate Gmos-S (“S” for *single* binary mask prediction), which predicts all moving objects into a single foreground mask. Gmos-S shares the encoders, feature fusion, and self-attention module with the Gmos proposer, but (i) removes the query-based transformer decoder, (ii) replaces the per-query mask head with a single convolutional decoder that outputs one binary foreground mask per frame, and (iii) dispenses with the follow-up propagator entirely. This makes Gmos-S an end-to-end model that produces instantaneous (per-frame) motion segmentation and achieves lower inference latency than Gmos. Full architectural details are provided in Appendix [A.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A1.SS1 "A.1 Gmos-S ‣ Appendix A Additional method details ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time").

For every frame tt, the proposer yields a set of NN candidate tuples {(M^t(i),m^t(i),u^t(i),c^t(i))}i=1N\{(\hat{M}^{(i)}\_{t},\hat{m}^{(i)}\_{t},\hat{u}^{(i)}\_{t},\hat{c}^{(i)}\_{t})\}\_{i=1}^{N}. The role of the propagator is to lift these per-frame proposals {M^t(i)}\{\hat{M}^{(i)}\_{t}\} into coherent object tracks across the full video, guided by the predicted motion probabilities {m^t(i)}\{\hat{m}^{(i)}\_{t}\} and estimated IoUs {u^t(i)}\{\hat{u}^{(i)}\_{t}\}. The confidence scores {c^t(i)}\{\hat{c}^{(i)}\_{t}\} are not used here, as they primarily serve as regularisers during proposer training. We build this process on a SAM2 video predictor [[55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib7 "SAM 2: segment anything in images and videos")] used as a mask-conditioned tracker, and define an elementary propagation step from which we build online and offline procedures.

Basic propagation step. Given a start frame and a direction, SAM2 propagates the currently tracked masks frame by frame. At each visited frame tt, the proposer predictions are first filtered by thresholding on the motion probabilities {m^t(i)}\{\hat{m}^{(i)}\_{t}\} and estimated IoUs {u^t(i)}\{\hat{u}^{(i)}\_{t}\}. The remaining high-quality moving-object proposals are then matched to the propagated masks via Hungarian assignment based on mask IoU, and the set of active tracks is updated according to one of two cases:

* • Addition. If a proposer prediction matches no existing SAM2 track, it is instantiated as a new mask track starting from frame tt. * • Reinforcement. If a proposer prediction matches an existing SAM2 track at high IoU, it is injected as an additional prompt for that track, suppressing drift.
Addition. If a proposer prediction matches no existing SAM2 track, it is instantiated as a new mask track starting from frame tt.
Reinforcement. If a proposer prediction matches an existing SAM2 track at high IoU, it is injected as an additional prompt for that track, suppressing drift.

For both cases above, the track’s motion state at frame tt is set to moving. Conversely, if an existing track has a propagated mask at frame tt but no proposer prediction falls on the same region (e.g. the object was moving earlier but has become static), the track’s motion state at frame tt is set to static.

Online procedure. The online procedure initialises the tracker from the *first frame* and runs the basic propagation steps in a single causal forward pass. This streams a mask and motion state for each frame as soon as it is processed, supporting MOS-I. Since the sequence is viewed only once and causally, masks cannot be recovered for frames preceding an object’s first observed motion, making the online procedure incompatible with the conventional MOS setting that requires a mask at every frame.

Offline procedure. The offline procedure builds on top of the online results with a second propagation stage. It first selects an *anchor frame* t⋆t^{\star} from the online output, defined as the frame whose moving object proposals carry the highest aggregate predicted IoU. The basic propagation step is then run *bi-directionally*, forward from t⋆t^{\star} to TT and backward from t⋆t^{\star} to 11, yielding a dense mask for every object at every frame. This mode can be used for both MOS and MOS-I. Further algorithmic details and pseudo-code are provided in Appendix [A.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A1.SS2 "A.2 Gmos propagator ‣ Appendix A Additional method details ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time").

We introduce Gmos-2K, a video moving object segmentation dataset with temporally fine-grained motion labels. Beyond ground-truth masks for moving objects, it specifies the exact temporal windows during which each object is in motion, enabling precise training and evaluation of time-sensitive motion segmentation methods.

Curation pipeline. Temporal motion labels are substantially cheaper to obtain than dense segmentation masks. We therefore build upon five existing video object segmentation datasets (DAVIS17 [[53](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib2 "The 2017 davis challenge on video object segmentation")], YTVOS19 [[67](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib3 "Youtube-vos: a large-scale video object segmentation benchmark")], OVIS [[54](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib67 "Occluded video instance segmentation: a benchmark")], MoCA-Mask [[11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib65 "Implicit motion handling for video camouflaged object detection")], and HOI4D [[40](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib66 "HOI4D: a 4d egocentric dataset for category-level human-object interaction")]) and annotate them with per-object motion timestamps. [Fig.˜3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S3.F3 "In 3 Dataset: Gmos-2K ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") (left) illustrates the data filtering and annotation pipeline. Starting from 5,0015{,}001 candidate videos, we apply two sequential filters:

1. (i) Do all independently moving objects in the video have ground-truth segmentation masks? If yes, the sequence proceeds to the second question, otherwise it is filtered out. Note, an object is considered “moving” if it undergoes motion independent of the camera for at least one frame. This question concerns only moving-object masks. Static objects without masks are permissible. 2. (ii) Are all annotated objects moving throughout the entire sequence? If yes, no additional annotation is needed. Otherwise, the video is forwarded for Temporally Fine-grained Annotation (TFA).

Temporally Fine-grained Annotation (TFA). Given a video sequence, TFA aims to annotate time intervals on the temporal axis that specify when objects are moving, with each object annotated independently. The annotation process follows that for video temporal grounding. Further details on the annotation interface, guidelines, and quality controls are provided in Appendix [D](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A4 "Appendix D Gmos-2K curation details ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time").

Dataset statistics. Gmos-2K comprises 2,2102{,}210 videos with 4,6484{,}648 annotated moving objects, drawn from five constituent subsets that span diverse domains: heavily occluded scenes (OVIS), hand-object interactions (HOI4D), and wildlife and human-centric clips (DAVIS17, YTVOS19, MoCA-Mask). Example sequences are shown in [Fig.˜C2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A3.F2 "In Appendix C Dataset details ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time"), with instantaneously moving objects labelled.

The pie charts in [Fig.˜3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S3.F3 "In 3 Dataset: Gmos-2K ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") (right) show the per-subset distribution of videos and objects. OVIS contributes a disproportionately large share of objects, reflecting its dense multi-object scenes. The accompanying histograms characterise two complementary aspects of the dataset. The per-video object count (top) concentrates on sequences with 0–44 moving objects, with a long tail extending beyond 44. The motion proportion (bottom), defined as the fraction of frames in which an object is actively moving, peaks at fully moving objects, with the remaining cases distributed roughly uniformly across lower values.

The training and test splits consist of 1,9301{,}930 and 280280 videos, respectively. All five subsets contribute to the training split, while DAVIS17 and YTVOS19 additionally contribute to the test split designed for MOS-I evaluation, renamed DAVIS17-IM and YTVOS19-IM (“IM” for Instantaneous Motion) to distinguish them from the conventional MOS datasets. Full per-subset statistics are reported in [Tab.˜C1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A3.T1 "In Appendix C Dataset details ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time").

We train Gmos on a composite dataset of 14,17114{,}171 videos (782782K annotated frames), combining three data sources. (i) Synthetic data. Kubric [[20](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib62 "Kubric: a scalable dataset generator")], PointOdyssey [[77](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib63 "PointOdyssey: a large-scale synthetic dataset for long-term point tracking")], and DynamicReplica [[25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib64 "DynamicStereo: consistent dynamic depth from stereo videos")] provide 10,52610{,}526 videos with pixel-perfect ground truth and motion labels. (ii) Real moving-object data (Gmos-2K). The five Gmos-2K training subsets ([Sec.˜3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S3 "3 Dataset: Gmos-2K ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time")) contribute 1,9301{,}930 real-world videos with temporally fine-grained motion labels. (iii) Real static-scene data. 1,7151{,}715 clips from the Mannequin Challenge dataset [[34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib68 "Learning the depths of moving people by watching frozen people")], in which people remain frozen while the camera moves freely, provide static-scene supervision that teaches the model to distinguish depth parallax from independent object motion. The detailed per-dataset statistics are provided in [Tab.˜C1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A3.T1 "In Appendix C Dataset details ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time").
We evaluate Gmos on the following video object segmentation tasks.

Moving Object Segmentation (MOS) predicts, at every frame, a segmentation mask for every object that moves at any point in the sequence, regardless of its per-frame motion state. We evaluate on established MOS benchmarks: DAVIS16-M [[22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib61 "Segment any motion in videos")] (“M” for “Moving”), DAVIS17-M [[14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib37 "Towards segmenting anything that moves")], SegTrackv2 [[32](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib69 "Video segmentation by tracking many figure-ground segments")], FBMS-59 [[46](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib70 "Segmentation of moving objects by long term video analysis")], and MoCA [Lamdouar20], along with YTVOS19-M, a new benchmark derived from the Gmos-2K test set. Following standard practice, all benchmarks report region similarity 𝒥\mathcal{J} and contour accuracy ℱ\mathcal{F}, except MoCA, which uses detection success rate (SR) [Yang21a].

MOS-I (“I” for *instantaneous*) is a temporally fine-grained evaluation protocol for MOS that (i) retains the sequence-level object identity association of MOS, (ii) scores segmentation masks only on frames where an object is actively moving, and (iii) explicitly penalises false-positive predictions on static or background objects. We instantiate it on two new benchmarks derived from the Gmos-2K test set, namely DAVIS17-IM and YTVOS19-IM (“IM” for “Instantaneous Motion”), and report performance on three complementary metrics.

* • Moving-object Jaccard (𝒥mov{\mathcal{J}\_{\text{mov}}}) – segmentation accuracy on actively moving frames. For each annotated object, 𝒥\mathcal{J} is averaged over the frames in which it is labelled as moving in Gmos-2K. * • False-positive count (FP count) – penalisation of static and background predictions. We measure the average number of static or background objects per frame that are incorrectly predicted as moving. While 𝒥mov\mathcal{J}\_{\text{mov}} rewards detecting true motion, FP count penalises spurious motion claims. * • Mean temporal IoU (mtIoU) – joint measure of moving-object detection and false-positive suppression. For each sequence, we compute a temporal IoU between predicted and ground-truth moving objects, counted per object per frame. The *union* covers all (object, frame) entries marked as moving by either the prediction or the ground truth. The *intersection* covers entries where a predicted and a ground-truth moving object are matched by region similarity 𝒥\mathcal{J} at threshold kk. Sweeping k∈{0.5,0.55,…,0.95}k\in\{0.5,0.55,\dots,0.95\} and averaging the resulting tIoUs yields the final mtIoU.

Moving-object Jaccard (𝒥mov{\mathcal{J}\_{\text{mov}}}) – segmentation accuracy on actively moving frames. For each annotated object, 𝒥\mathcal{J} is averaged over the frames in which it is labelled as moving in Gmos-2K.

Unsupervised Video Object Segmentation (UVOS) requires automatically segmenting salient objects in a video, where targets are defined by perceptual salience and need not be moving. We report results on DAVIS16 [[52](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib1 "A benchmark dataset and evaluation methodology for video object segmentation")] and DAVIS17 [[53](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib2 "The 2017 davis challenge on video object segmentation")] using the standard region similarity 𝒥\mathcal{J} and contour accuracy ℱ\mathcal{F}.

We detail the design choices of Gmos below. Further implementation details are provided in Appendix [B](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A2 "Appendix B Additional implementation details ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time"), alongside a comprehensive ablation study in Appendix [E](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A5 "Appendix E Ablation study ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time").

Architecture. Gmos uses pretrained π3\pi^{3} [[64](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib54 "π3: Permutation-equivariant visual geometry learning")] (DINOv2 [[49](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib72 "DINOv2: learning robust visual features without supervision")] ViT-L/14) and SAM2 [[55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib7 "SAM 2: segment anything in images and videos")] (Hiera-L [[57](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib73 "Hiera: a hierarchical vision transformer without the bells-and-whistles")]) as the geometric and segmentation encoders, both kept frozen. Bottleneck features have spatial resolution 64×6464{\times}64 and channel dimension 256256. The trainable transformer encoder and decoder each have 33 layers and 88 attention heads. We use 100100 object queries and predict masks at 256×256256{\times}256.

Input setting. The Gmos proposer operates on 55 frames sampled uniformly from a temporal window centred on the target frame. The window size is randomly sampled between 0.160.16 s and 1.001.00 s during training to expose the model to a range of motion speeds, and fixed at 0.50.5 s at inference.

Training setup. We optimise with AdamW [[41](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib71 "Decoupled weight decay regularization")] using learning rate 1×10−41{\times}10^{-4}, weight decay 0.010.01, gradient clipping at norm 1.01.0, and a cosine schedule with 2,0002{,}000 warmup steps. Training runs on 22 NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs for approximately 22 days, with an effective batch size of 88. For the proposer loss in [Eq.˜2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S2.E2 "In 2.1 Gmos proposer ‣ 2 Method: Gmos ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time"), we set (λmask,λmotion,λiou,λconfmov,λconfsta)=(20, 1, 1, 0.1, 0.001)(\lambda\_{\text{mask}},\,\lambda\_{\text{motion}},\,\lambda\_{\text{iou}},\,\lambda^{\text{mov}}\_{\text{conf}},\,\lambda^{\text{sta}}\_{\text{conf}})=(20,\>1,\>1,\>0.1,\>0.001), with a rescaled confidence upper bound cmax=5c\_{\text{max}}=5. The mask loss combines focal (α=0.25\alpha{=}0.25, γ=2\gamma{=}2) and dice losses in a 20:120{:}1 ratio.

[Tab.˜2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S4.T2 "In 4.3 Implementation details ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") reports results on the conventional MOS setting, where moving-object masks are predicted at the sequence level. Gmos, and its foreground–background variant Gmos-S, achieves new state-of-the-art performance across all benchmarks. Gains are most pronounced on YTVOS19-M, whose denser and more varied object interactions expose the limitations of prior flow- and trajectory-based methods. Gmos also remains robust on camouflaged objects (MoCA), where segmentation must rely exclusively on motion cues.

Since prior methods treat motion as a sequence-level attribute and cannot capture instantaneous motion states, Gmos surpasses them by a substantial margin on all three metrics. We additionally evaluate an online variant of Gmos ([Sec.˜2.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S2.SS2 "2.2 Gmos propagator ‣ 2 Method: Gmos ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time")), which performs on par with the default offline mode. The offline mode’s second global propagation even slightly hurts FP count and mtIoU, as the bidirectional pass amplifies any borderline false positives from the first pass. The online mode, however, is restricted to the MOS-I setup, since a single forward pass cannot recover masks for objects that are initially static and only later begin to move. The offline procedure therefore remains our default across all tasks, including MOS and UVOS.

We also report performance on Unsupervised Video Object Segmentation (UVOS), which targets the prediction of salient objects regardless of their motion state. Although UVOS lies outside our primary focus of segmenting only moving objects, [Tab.˜4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S4.T4 "In 4.4 Quantitative results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") shows that Gmos generalises well to this adjacent task, achieving state-of-the-art results on the multi-object DAVIS17 benchmark and remaining on par with the prior best on the single-object DAVIS16.

Motion Segmentation (MS) seeks to separate independently moving regions from the static background, producing a binary foreground–background mask. Mainstream approaches take optical flow as the motion signal and cluster pixels according to similar motion patterns [[50](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib33 "Fast object segmentation in unconstrained video"), [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib34 "It’s moving! a probabilistic model for causal motion segmentation in moving camera videos"), [60](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib35 "Learning video object segmentation with visual memory"), [61](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib36 "Learning to segment moving objects"), Yang21a, Lamdouar20, [14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib37 "Towards segmenting anything that moves"), [69](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib38 "DyStaB: unsupervised object segmentation via dynamic-static bootstrapping"), Choudhury22, [70](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib39 "Unsupervised moving object detection via contextual information separation"), [43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib40 "EM-driven unsupervised learning for efficient motion segmentation"), [44](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib41 "Unsupervised motion segmentation in one go: smooth long-term model over a video")]. However, these flow-based approaches are inherently bound by the quality of the pre-computed optical flow, and also vulnerable to large camera motion and induced depth parallax. A complementary line of work aggregates motion cues over longer temporal windows via point trajectories [[2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib42 "Object segmentation by long term analysis of point trajectories"), [47](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib43 "Object segmentation in video: a hierarchical variational approach for turning point trajectories into dense regions"), [26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib44 "Motion trajectory segmentation via minimum cost multicuts"), [18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib45 "Video segmentation by tracing discontinuities in a trajectory embedding")]. Recent advances in point tracking [Karaev25, [15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib46 "TAP-vid: a benchmark for tracking any point in a video"), [16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib47 "TAPIR: tracking any point with per-frame initialization and temporal refinement")] have substantially improved long-range correspondence, enabling segmentation to be learnt directly from dense trajectories [Karazija24b, [22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib61 "Segment any motion in videos")]. However, such reliance on long-term tracking makes these methods insensitive to static–dynamic transitions, limiting their online applicability.

Another line of work exploits 3D or 4D geometric priors for motion segmentation. MegaSAM [[35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib51 "MegaSaM: accurate, fast and robust structure and motion from casual dynamic videos")] learns motion probability maps from estimated camera parameters and depth to separate moving and static content, while RoMo [[19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib52 "RoMo: robust motion segmentation improves structure from motion")] combines optical flow with epipolar constraints and iteratively refines motion masks using segmentation priors from SAM [[27](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib19 "Segment anything")]. Building upon feed-forward reconstruction methods [[62](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib48 "DUSt3R: geometric 3d vision made easy"), Wang25], MonST3R [[74](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib55 "MonST3r: a simple approach for estimating geometry in the presence of motion")] and DAS3R [[66](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib49 "DAS3R: dynamics-aware gaussian splatting for static scene reconstruction")] jointly decode moving regions alongside temporally consistent video reconstructions. Easi3R [[6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib50 "Easi3R: estimating disentangled motion from dust3r without training")] reveals that the attention layers of such reconstruction models already encode relative camera-object motion. GeoMotion [[21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib53 "GeoMotion: rethinking motion segmentation via latent 4d geometry")] further exploits the latent 4D features of π3\pi^{3} [[64](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib54 "π3: Permutation-equivariant visual geometry learning")] to directly disentangle object and camera motion in a feed-forward manner.

Moving Object Segmentation (MOS) aims to discover, segment, and track individual moving objects. For videos containing a single moving object, MOS degenerates to foreground–background motion segmentation. Recent works instead focus on the more challenging multi-object scenario, similarly building upon the aforementioned motion cues (i.e. flow, trajectories, and geometric priors).

Without relying on human annotations, one group of methods [[58](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib57 "Multi-object discovery by low-dimensional object motion"), [36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib59 "Bootstrapping objectness from videos by relaxed common fate and visual grouping"), [28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib60 "Divided attention: unsupervised multi-object discovery with contextually separated slots")] pursues purely unsupervised training via flow reconstruction as a proxy objective. Alternatively, OCLR [Xie22] takes optical flow as input and trains object-centric layered representations on synthetic data to discover and track multiple objects under occlusion, while ABR [Xie24] extends it with appearance-based refinement.

With increasingly available annotated masks and strong pre-trained models, FlowSAM [Xie24a] injects optical flow into SAM [[27](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib19 "Segment anything")], either as an input channel or as prompt signals, for moving object segmentation. SegAnyMo [[22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib61 "Segment any motion in videos")] fuses long-range trajectory cues with DINO [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib58 "Emerging properties in self-supervised vision transformers")] features and employs SAM2 [[55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib7 "SAM 2: segment anything in images and videos")] for mask densification.

We presented Gmos, a feed-forward framework that grounds Moving Object Segmentation in 3D space and time, making it robust to camera-induced parallax in space and temporally sensitive to per-frame motion-state changes. Gmos operates on RGB video alone and supports both online and offline inference. To facilitate training and evaluation in this regime, we curated Gmos-2K, a real-world video dataset with per-object temporal motion annotations, and formalised MOS-I, a temporally fine-grained evaluation protocol with three complementary metrics. Gmos achieves state-of-the-art results on MOS, MOS-I, and UVOS benchmarks, while running roughly three times faster than prior MOS methods.

Architecture. Gmos-S is designed as a streaming foreground–background variant of the Gmos proposer. As illustrated in [Fig.˜A1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A1.F1 "In A.1 Gmos-S ‣ Appendix A Additional method details ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time"), it shares the frozen geometric encoder (π3\pi^{3}), the frozen segmentation encoder (SAM2), and the feature fusion module with the Gmos proposer ([Fig.˜2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S2.F2 "In 2.1 Gmos proposer ‣ 2 Method: Gmos ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time")). Two design choices distinguish it from the full proposer: (i) the transformer decoder and the NN learnable object queries are removed, and the fused feature is passed directly through an upsampling decoder that predicts a single binary foreground–background mask per frame; and (ii) since motion is implicit in the union of moving objects, the motion head is dropped, and the remaining confidence and IoU heads operate on globally average-pooled fused features, producing one scalar per frame instead of one per object.

In addition, we dispense with the propagator, as no object-level proposals are produced by Gmos-S. Predictions are therefore instantaneous and online, making Gmos-S the fastest variant in our framework.

children.heading: D.1 Instructions and tools for annotators

content.text: Video-level filtering. As described in [Sec.˜3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S3 "3 Dataset: Gmos-2K ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time"), the curation pipeline begins by filtering 5,0015{,}001 candidate videos through two sequential questions: (i) whether all independently moving objects have ground-truth segmentation masks, and (ii) whether all annotated objects are moving throughout the entire sequence. Annotators review each video and label their answers accordingly. The detailed instructions provided to annotators are shown below.

Temporally Fine-grained Annotation (TFA). Videos that pass the first filter but fail the second are forwarded for TFA, which labels per-object motion intervals along the temporal axis. We perform TFA using VIA [Dutta19a], an open-source annotation tool with built-in temporal grounding functionality. As shown in [Fig.˜D3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A4.F3 "In D.1 Instructions and tools for annotators ‣ Appendix D Gmos-2K curation details ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time"), we adapt the default VIA interface with two modifications: (i) the original video and its mask-overlaid counterpart are displayed side-by-side, with each object assigned a unique colour for easy identification; and (ii) the temporal axes are colour-coded to correspond to individual objects. The detailed annotation workflow and instructions are provided below.
Quality control. We apply quality control protocols at each of the above stages.

* • Video-level filtering. Two annotators independently answer the two filtering questions for each candidate video. Sequences on which they disagree are flagged and jointly reviewed until a consensus is reached, ensuring that no qualifying video is dropped and no unsuitable video is forwarded to TFA. * • Temporally Fine-grained Annotation (TFA). After each sequence is annotated, a second annotator visualises the resulting MOS-I ground truth, with each object’s mask overlaid only on the frames within its labelled motion intervals. The reviewer checks for (i) moving objects whose motion intervals are missing entirely (an object never receives a mask despite moving), (ii) static or background objects falsely labelled as moving (a mask appears on frames where the object is at rest), and (iii) inaccurate motion–rest transition boundaries. This step also captures errors from the filtering stage, removing any unsuitable videos that erroneously passed the previous filter. Flagged cases are returned to the original annotator for revision and re-verified by the reviewer.

To probe the proposer directly, we skip the propagator and apply per-frame Hungarian matching between proposer outputs and the ground truth, reporting performance on DAVIS17-IM.

Geometric and segmentation encoders. [Tab.˜E3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A5.T3 "In E.1 Ablations on Gmos proposer ‣ Appendix E Ablation study ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") ablates the encoder choices for the Gmos proposer. Removing the geometric encoder destroys the model’s grounding ability, producing many hallucinated false positives. Replacing π3\pi^{3} with VGGT or DA3 yields a modest drop, suggesting that π3\pi^{3} provides richer 4D priors that better disentangle object motion from camera motion.

Dropping the segmentation encoder, on the other hand, reduces the false-positive count but substantially degrades mask quality, causing large drops in mtIoU and 𝒥mov\mathcal{J}\_{\text{mov}}. Replacing SAM2 with the more recent SAM3 [[3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib22 "SAM 3: segment anything with concepts")] yields comparable mask quality and only a marginal 𝒥mov\mathcal{J}\_{\text{mov}} gain. We therefore retain SAM2 as the default segmentation encoder for direct comparison with prior methods that also build on it.

Training dataset composition. [Tab.˜E4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A5.T4 "In E.1 Ablations on Gmos proposer ‣ Appendix E Ablation study ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") investigates how the major subsets contribute to training. Synthetic data alone yields a strong proposer with a low FP count, but limited mtIoU and 𝒥mov\mathcal{J}\_{\text{mov}} due to the synthetic-to-real domain gap. Adding the real moving-object data from Gmos-2K substantially improves segmentation quality, while the static-scene Mannequin Challenge clips further reduce the FP count by teaching the model to suppress false motion induced by depth parallax.

Confidence-based loss. [Tab.˜E5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A5.T5 "In E.1 Ablations on Gmos proposer ‣ Appendix E Ablation study ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") shows that the confidence-based loss improves all three metrics by mitigating noisy motion annotations near static–moving transitions.

Inference temporal window size. [Tab.˜E6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A5.T6 "In Tab. E7 ‣ E.1 Ablations on Gmos proposer ‣ Appendix E Ablation study ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") varies the temporal window from which five input frames are uniformly sampled at inference. Since the proposer is trained with variable window lengths, performance remains relatively stable across settings. In particular, a larger window makes moving objects easier to discover (raising 𝒥mov\mathcal{J}\_{\text{mov}}) but reduces temporal granularity, resulting in more false positives. A window of ∼0.5\sim 0.5 s strikes the best balance, achieving the highest mtIoU.

Input frame gap. [Tab.˜E7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A5.T7 "In E.1 Ablations on Gmos proposer ‣ Appendix E Ablation study ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") replaces the uniformly sampling frame gap (i.e. “1 1 1 1”) with non-uniform gaps that emphasise the centre frame. Non-uniform gaps slightly improve 𝒥mov\mathcal{J}\_{\text{mov}} on moving objects but consistently raise FP count, suggesting that uniform sampling provides the most balanced motion cues for the proposer.

Fusing early-layer π3\pi^{3} features. By default, the Gmos proposer takes two feature sources as input, geometric (the last layer of the π3\pi^{3} encoder) and segmentation (the last layer of the SAM2 encoder). We investigate whether adding a *third* source, early-layer signals from the π3\pi^{3} encoder, improves the proposer. As outlined in [Tab.˜E9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A5.T9 "In E.1 Ablations on Gmos proposer ‣ Appendix E Ablation study ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time"), we consider two modes, both sampling early-layer π3\pi^{3} signals from layers 77, 1515, 2323, and 3131 (of 3636). In *feature* mode, activations from the sampled layers are concatenated and projected. In *attention* mode, cross-attention maps between the middle frame and all other frames are concatenated and projected to form the additional signal.

[Tab.˜E9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A5.T9 "In E.1 Ablations on Gmos proposer ‣ Appendix E Ablation study ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") shows that both variants perform on par with the default, indicating that the final-layer π3\pi^{3} feature alone already suffices for motion reasoning. We therefore retain only the final-layer π3\pi^{3} feature as the geometric input.

Mask decoder. As detailed in [Fig.˜2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S2.F2 "In 2.1 Gmos proposer ‣ 2 Method: Gmos ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time"), the Gmos proposer employs a trainable hypernetwork mask decoder, in which the feature map is upsampled and attended by object embeddings.

An alternative is to discard the upsampler and predict masks directly at the bottleneck resolution (64×6464{\times}64), using off-the-shelf SAM2 to recover the full-resolution mask for each object. Specifically, we randomly sample 1010 positive and 33 negative points from the low-resolution prediction of each object as prompts to SAM2.

[Tab.˜E9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A5.T9 "In E.1 Ablations on Gmos proposer ‣ Appendix E Ablation study ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") compares our lightweight trainable upsampling decoder against this SAM2-based decoding. The latter underperforms on all metrics, suggesting that the low-resolution prediction does not fully capture moving-object information.

[Tab.˜E10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A5.T10 "In E.2 Ablations on Gmos propagator ‣ Appendix E Ablation study ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") investigates the start-frame strategy for each propagation stage in the Gmos propagator. Exp. A corresponds to our default online setup, with a single forward propagation starting at frame 11. Since the sequence is traversed only once in temporal order, masks cannot be recovered for every frame (e.g. an object initially static but moves later). Therefore, Gmos (online) is restricted to the MOS-I setup.

The four remaining variants (Exp. B–E) add a second propagation stage, enabling both MOS-I and MOS evaluation. Among these, Exp. C and D start the first propagation from a selected anchor frame and perform slightly better overall, but they sacrifice causality in the first propagation stage. We therefore adopt Exp. E as our offline default, since its first stage coincides with the online procedure and its second stage further refines the result via a curated prompt set.

The training of Gmos proposer is stochastic, while the propagator step is fully deterministic. We repeat the proposer training with four different random seeds (Exp. A–D), report the per-frame Hungarian-matched results in the left half of [Tab.˜E11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A5.T11 "In E.2 Ablations on Gmos propagator ‣ Appendix E Ablation study ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time"), and apply the deterministic propagator on top of each to obtain the sequence-level (object ID associated) results in the right half. The small standard deviations on both halves indicate that Gmos is statistically stable across seeds, and the propagator brings consistent gains over the proposer alone in every run.

We provide additional qualitative results to complement [Figs.˜4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S4.F4 "In 4.5 Qualitative results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") and [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S4.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ 4.5 Qualitative results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") in the main paper. [Fig.˜F4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A6.F4 "In Appendix F Additional qualitative visualisations ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") shows further comparisons against representative baselines under the multi-object and foreground–background protocols, and [Fig.˜F5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A6.F5 "In Appendix F Additional qualitative visualisations ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") illustrates Gmos’s behaviour on more in-the-wild sequences, distinguishing between MOS-I and MOS predictions.

Failure cases. [Fig.˜G6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A7.F6 "In Appendix G Discussion ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") illustrates two representative failure modes, both stemming from the limited spatial granularity of the π3\pi^{3} geometric backbone. The left example (a table football game) shows a scene with many fast-moving objects under heavy occlusion. Gmos misses several small moving instances in the background, suggesting that the backbone struggles with fine-grained moving-object discovery in cluttered scenes. The right example shows a driving scene in which a large reflective truck passes the camera. Although the truck is static, Gmos incorrectly predicts it as moving at a particular frame, exposing limitations of the backbone in per-object motion-state prediction under reflections and extreme depth parallax.

Possible extensions. We outline two natural directions for future work. First, the geometric backbone could be fine-tuned on larger and more diverse motion-annotated datasets to strengthen both fine-grained moving-object discovery and motion-state prediction. Second, the proposer and propagator could be merged into a single end-to-end trainable framework, allowing the temporal consistency signal to improve mask quality and yield more accurate motion-state predictions over long videos.

Broader impact. Gmos enables real-time identification of moving objects directly from RGB video, supporting safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving, ecological and biomedical monitoring, public-safety surveillance, and dynamic 3D/4D scene reconstruction for robotics and AR/VR. Operating without pre-computed flow or trajectories also lowers the compute footprint of motion-aware perception. We release Gmos-2K and the MOS-I protocol for reproducible research. As with any video-segmentation system, Gmos could be misused in surveillance contexts that raise privacy concerns, particularly when combined with identity-recognition tools. We encourage downstream users to comply with data-protection regulations and obtain appropriate consent.

###### Abstract

Moving Object Segmentation (MOS) aims to discover, segment, and track objects that move independently of the camera. Current MOS methods, however, exhibit two fundamental limitations: they rely on pre-computed 2D auxiliary modalities such as optical flow or point trajectories that lack 3D geometric information, and they treat motion as a sequence-level attribute, overlooking the instantaneous motion state of each object. ## 1 Introduction

Moving object segmentation (MOS) aims to discover, segment, and track objects that move independently of the camera. This capability is foundational to applications such as autonomous driving [[5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib77 "Moving object segmentation in 3D LiDAR data: a learning-based approach exploiting sequential data"), [33](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib78 "Multi-sensor fusion for robust localization with moving object segmentation in complex dynamic 3D scenes")], camouflaged object detection [Lamdouar20, Yang21a], and video surveillance [[45](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib76 "Deep anomaly detection through visual attention in surveillance videos"), [65](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib79 "Attention-based temporal encoding network with background-independent motion mask for action recognition")], and has become increasingly central to recent 3D/4D scene reconstruction methods [[35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib51 "MegaSaM: accurate, fast and robust structure and motion from casual dynamic videos"), [19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib52 "RoMo: robust motion segmentation improves structure from motion")] that require motion masks to separate dynamic objects from the static scene.

Current MOS methods exhibit two fundamental limitations, as outlined in [Tab.˜1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S1.T1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time"). *First*, they are not 3D-aware and remain fragile under large camera motion or depth parallax. This stems from their heavy reliance on pre-computed 2D auxiliary modalities (e.g. optical flow [Yang21a, Xie22, [36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib59 "Bootstrapping objectness from videos by relaxed common fate and visual grouping")] or point trajectories [[22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib61 "Segment any motion in videos"), Karazija24b]), which lack 3D geometric information and incur substantial pre-processing overhead. *Second*, existing benchmarks assume that objects move throughout the video, leading methods to treat motion as a *sequence-level* attribute and to overlook the instantaneous motion state of each object. This coarse temporal granularity precludes online and real-time deployment.

We address both limitations by grounding MOS in *space* and *time*. Our approach rests on two observations: (i) the geometric representations learnt by recent feed-forward 3D reconstruction models already encode sufficient information to disentangle camera and object motion, and (ii) independent object motion is reliably identifiable from a short temporal window (∼\sim0.50.5 s).

Building on these insights, we propose Gmos, a proposer–propagator framework that operates directly on RGB video without any auxiliary pre-computed modalities. A per-frame *proposer* fuses geometric features from a π3\pi^{3} encoder [[64](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib54 "π3: Permutation-equivariant visual geometry learning")] with segmentation features from a SAM2 encoder [[55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib7 "SAM 2: segment anything in images and videos")], jointly producing object mask proposals and per-frame motion-state predictions. A SAM2-based *propagator* then links these proposals into consistent tracks across frames. We further introduce Gmos-S (“S” for *single*), a streaming foreground–background variant that predicts all moving objects as a *single binary* mask and dispenses with the propagator for even faster inference.

As shown in [Tab.˜4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S4.T4 "In 4.4 Quantitative results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time"), performance gaps widen further on MOS-I, which requires predictions at finer temporal granularity. Since prior methods treat motion as a sequence-level attribute and cannot capture instantaneous motion states, Gmos surpasses them by a substantial margin on all three metrics. We additionally evaluate an online variant of Gmos ([Sec.˜2.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S2.SS2 "2.2 Gmos propagator ‣ 2 Method: Gmos ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time")), which performs on par with the default offline mode. This can be attributed to the instantaneous nature of MOS-I, where a short causal window already provides sufficient motion evidence. The offline mode’s second global propagation even slightly hurts FP count and mtIoU, as the bidirectional pass amplifies any borderline false positives from the first pass. The online mode, however, is restricted to the MOS-I setup, since a single forward pass cannot recover masks for objects that are initially static and only later begin to move. The offline procedure therefore remains our default across all tasks, including MOS and UVOS.

We also report performance on Unsupervised Video Object Segmentation (UVOS), which targets the prediction of salient objects regardless of their motion state. Although UVOS lies outside our primary focus of segmenting only moving objects, [Tab.˜4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S4.T4 "In 4.4 Quantitative results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") shows that Gmos generalises well to this adjacent task, achieving state-of-the-art results on the multi-object DAVIS17 benchmark and remaining on par with the prior best on the single-object DAVIS16.

### 4.5 Qualitative results

[Fig.˜4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S4.F4 "In 4.5 Qualitative results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") compares Gmos against representative baselines on sequences from YTVOS19, DAVIS17, and MoCA. Regarding multi-object predictions, FlowSAM [Xie24a] tends to over-segment moving objects (e.g. treating the coral as moving), while SegAnyMo [[22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib61 "Segment any motion in videos")] misses moving objects or bleeds masks into the background. In contrast, Gmos assigns each moving object a consistent identity and boundary that closely follow the ground truth, even under heavy occlusion. Under the foreground–background protocol, GeoMotion [[21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib53 "GeoMotion: rethinking motion segmentation via latent 4d geometry")] captures prominent motion but overlooks instances near image boundaries (e.g. the right tiger), whereas Gmos-S recovers them reliably.

[Fig.˜5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S4.F5 "In 4.5 Qualitative results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") illustrates Gmos on in-the-wild videos, contrasting MOS-I and MOS predictions. In the left sequence, the meerkats become static mid-sequence. Our MOS-I predictions correctly identify the static states, while MOS produces consistent segmentation across frames. In the right sequence, a hand arranges fruits one piece at a time. Our MOS-I predictions correctly release each piece once it comes to rest, whereas MOS keeps them masked throughout.

## 5 Related works

Unsupervised Video Object Segmentation (UVOS) aims to identify salient objects in videos without any annotation at inference time, in contrast to semi-supervised VOS [[52](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib1 "A benchmark dataset and evaluation methodology for video object segmentation"), [53](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib2 "The 2017 davis challenge on video object segmentation"), [67](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib3 "Youtube-vos: a large-scale video object segmentation benchmark"), [48](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib4 "Video object segmentation using space-time memory networks"), [10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib5 "XMem: long-term video object segmentation with an atkinson-shiffrin memory model"), [72](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib6 "Decoupling features in hierarchical propagation for video object segmentation"), [8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib21 "Putting the object back into video object segmentation"), [55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib7 "SAM 2: segment anything in images and videos")], which propagates masks from first-frame ground truths. Early methods adopt two-stream architectures that fuse motion and appearance inputs [[23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib8 "Fusionseg: learning to combine motion and appearance for fully automatic segmentation of generic objects in videos"), [42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib9 "See more, know more: unsupervised video object segmentation with co-attention siamese networks"), [79](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib10 "Motion-attentive transition for zero-shot video object segmentation"), [68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib11 "Learning motion-appearance co-attention for zero-shot video object segmentation"), object segmentation"), [73](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib27 "Isomer: isomerous transformer for zero-shot video object segmentation"), prototype attention for unsupervised video object segmentation"), [30](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib31 "Guided slot attention for unsupervised video object segmentation"), [59](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib32 "Generalizable fourier augmentation for unsupervised video object segmentation")]. More recent works scale UVOS with new data strategies and modular pipeline designs: VideoCutLER [[63](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib17 "VideoCutLER: surprisingly simple unsupervised video instance segmentation")] scales training via copy-paste augmentation transferred from unsupervised image instance segmentation, DEVA [[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib18 "Tracking anything with decoupled video segmentation")] composes an image-level segmenter with a separate temporal propagator, and SAM-based approaches [[27](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib19 "Segment anything"), [55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib7 "SAM 2: segment anything in images and videos"), [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib22 "SAM 3: segment anything with concepts"), [76](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib20 "UVOSAM: a mask-free paradigm for unsupervised video object segmentation via segment anything model")] build UVOS pipelines around pre-trained foundation segmenters. Despite significant progress, UVOS methods typically target the most salient objects, which do not necessarily correspond to objects that are actually moving.

Motion Segmentation (MS) seeks to separate independently moving regions from the static background, producing a binary foreground–background mask. Mainstream approaches take optical flow as the motion signal and cluster pixels according to similar motion patterns [[50](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib33 "Fast object segmentation in unconstrained video"), [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib34 "It’s moving! a probabilistic model for causal motion segmentation in moving camera videos"), [60](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib35 "Learning video object segmentation with visual memory"), [61](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib36 "Learning to segment moving objects"), Yang21a, Lamdouar20, [14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib37 "Towards segmenting anything that moves"), [69](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib38 "DyStaB: unsupervised object segmentation via dynamic-static bootstrapping"), Choudhury22, [70](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib39 "Unsupervised moving object detection via contextual information separation"), [43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib40 "EM-driven unsupervised learning for efficient motion segmentation"), [44](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib41 "Unsupervised motion segmentation in one go: smooth long-term model over a video")]. However, these flow-based approaches are inherently bound by the quality of the pre-computed optical flow, and also vulnerable to large camera motion and induced depth parallax. A complementary line of work aggregates motion cues over longer temporal windows via point trajectories [[2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib42 "Object segmentation by long term analysis of point trajectories"), [47](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib43 "Object segmentation in video: a hierarchical variational approach for turning point trajectories into dense regions"), [26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib44 "Motion trajectory segmentation via minimum cost multicuts"), [18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib45 "Video segmentation by tracing discontinuities in a trajectory embedding")]. Recent advances in point tracking [Karaev25, [15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib46 "TAP-vid: a benchmark for tracking any point in a video"), [16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib47 "TAPIR: tracking any point with per-frame initialization and temporal refinement")] have substantially improved long-range correspondence, enabling segmentation to be learnt directly from dense trajectories [Karazija24b, [22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib61 "Segment any motion in videos")]. However, such reliance on long-term tracking makes these methods insensitive to static–dynamic transitions, limiting their online applicability.

Another line of work exploits 3D or 4D geometric priors for motion segmentation. MegaSAM [[35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib51 "MegaSaM: accurate, fast and robust structure and motion from casual dynamic videos")] learns motion probability maps from estimated camera parameters and depth to separate moving and static content, while RoMo [[19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib52 "RoMo: robust motion segmentation improves structure from motion")] combines optical flow with epipolar constraints and iteratively refines motion masks using segmentation priors from SAM [[27](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib19 "Segment anything")]. Building upon feed-forward reconstruction methods [[62](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib48 "DUSt3R: geometric 3d vision made easy"), Wang25], MonST3R [[74](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib55 "MonST3r: a simple approach for estimating geometry in the presence of motion")] and DAS3R [[66](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib49 "DAS3R: dynamics-aware gaussian splatting for static scene reconstruction")] jointly decode moving regions alongside temporally consistent video reconstructions. Easi3R [[6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib50 "Easi3R: estimating disentangled motion from dust3r without training")] reveals that the attention layers of such reconstruction models already encode relative camera-object motion. GeoMotion [[21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib53 "GeoMotion: rethinking motion segmentation via latent 4d geometry")] further exploits the latent 4D features of π3\pi^{3} [[64](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib54 "π3: Permutation-equivariant visual geometry learning")] to directly disentangle object and camera motion in a feed-forward manner.

π3\pi^{3}

Moving Object Segmentation (MOS) aims to discover, segment, and track individual moving objects. For videos containing a single moving object, MOS degenerates to foreground–background motion segmentation. Recent works instead focus on the more challenging multi-object scenario, similarly building upon the aforementioned motion cues (i.e. flow, trajectories, and geometric priors).

Without relying on human annotations, one group of methods [[58](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib57 "Multi-object discovery by low-dimensional object motion"), [36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib59 "Bootstrapping objectness from videos by relaxed common fate and visual grouping"), [28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib60 "Divided attention: unsupervised multi-object discovery with contextually separated slots")] pursues purely unsupervised training via flow reconstruction as a proxy objective. Alternatively, OCLR [Xie22] takes optical flow as input and trains object-centric layered representations on synthetic data to discover and track multiple objects under occlusion, while ABR [Xie24] extends it with appearance-based refinement.

With increasingly available annotated masks and strong pre-trained models, FlowSAM [Xie24a] injects optical flow into SAM [[27](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib19 "Segment anything")], either as an input channel or as prompt signals, for moving object segmentation. SegAnyMo [[22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib61 "Segment any motion in videos")] fuses long-range trajectory cues with DINO [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib58 "Emerging properties in self-supervised vision transformers")] features and employs SAM2 [[55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#bib.bib7 "SAM 2: segment anything in images and videos")] for mask densification.

## 6 Conclusion

We presented Gmos, a feed-forward framework that grounds Moving Object Segmentation in 3D space and time, making it robust to camera-induced parallax in space and temporally sensitive to per-frame motion-state changes. Gmos operates on RGB video alone and supports both online and offline inference. To facilitate training and evaluation in this regime, we curated Gmos-2K, a real-world video dataset with per-object temporal motion annotations, and formalised MOS-I, a temporally fine-grained evaluation protocol with three complementary metrics. Gmos achieves state-of-the-art results on MOS, MOS-I, and UVOS benchmarks, while running roughly three times faster than prior MOS methods.

### D.1 Instructions and tools for annotators

Video-level filtering. As described in [Sec.˜3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#S3 "3 Dataset: Gmos-2K ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time"), the curation pipeline begins by filtering 5,0015{,}001 candidate videos through two sequential questions: (i) whether all independently moving objects have ground-truth segmentation masks, and (ii) whether all annotated objects are moving throughout the entire sequence. Annotators review each video and label their answers accordingly. The detailed instructions provided to annotators are shown below.

5,0015{,}001

Temporally Fine-grained Annotation (TFA). Videos that pass the first filter but fail the second are forwarded for TFA, which labels per-object motion intervals along the temporal axis. We perform TFA using VIA [Dutta19a], an open-source annotation tool with built-in temporal grounding functionality. As shown in [Fig.˜D3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A4.F3 "In D.1 Instructions and tools for annotators ‣ Appendix D Gmos-2K curation details ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time"), we adapt the default VIA interface with two modifications: (i) the original video and its mask-overlaid counterpart are displayed side-by-side, with each object assigned a unique colour for easy identification; and (ii) the temporal axes are colour-coded to correspond to individual objects. The detailed annotation workflow and instructions are provided below.

Quality control. We apply quality control protocols at each of the above stages.

* • Video-level filtering. Two annotators independently answer the two filtering questions for each candidate video. Sequences on which they disagree are flagged and jointly reviewed until a consensus is reached, ensuring that no qualifying video is dropped and no unsuitable video is forwarded to TFA. * • Temporally Fine-grained Annotation (TFA). After each sequence is annotated, a second annotator visualises the resulting MOS-I ground truth, with each object’s mask overlaid only on the frames within its labelled motion intervals. The reviewer checks for (i) moving objects whose motion intervals are missing entirely (an object never receives a mask despite moving), (ii) static or background objects falsely labelled as moving (a mask appears on frames where the object is at rest), and (iii) inaccurate motion–rest transition boundaries. This step also captures errors from the filtering stage, removing any unsuitable videos that erroneously passed the previous filter. Flagged cases are returned to the original annotator for revision and re-verified by the reviewer.

### E.3 Repeating experiments

The training of Gmos proposer is stochastic, while the propagator step is fully deterministic. We repeat the proposer training with four different random seeds (Exp. A–D), report the per-frame Hungarian-matched results in the left half of [Tab.˜E11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A5.T11 "In E.2 Ablations on Gmos propagator ‣ Appendix E Ablation study ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time"), and apply the deterministic propagator on top of each to obtain the sequence-level (object ID associated) results in the right half. The small standard deviations on both halves indicate that Gmos is statistically stable across seeds, and the propagator brings consistent gains over the proposer alone in every run.

## Appendix G Discussion

Failure cases. [Fig.˜G6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30352#A7.F6 "In Appendix G Discussion ‣ Gmos: Grounding Moving Object Segmentation in 3D Space and Time") illustrates two representative failure modes, both stemming from the limited spatial granularity of the π3\pi^{3} geometric backbone. The left example (a table football game) shows a scene with many fast-moving objects under heavy occlusion. Gmos misses several small moving instances in the background, suggesting that the backbone struggles with fine-grained moving-object discovery in cluttered scenes. The right example shows a driving scene in which a large reflective truck passes the camera. Although the truck is static, Gmos incorrectly predicts it as moving at a particular frame, exposing limitations of the backbone in per-object motion-state prediction under reflections and extreme depth parallax.

π3\pi^{3}

Possible extensions. We outline two natural directions for future work. First, the geometric backbone could be fine-tuned on larger and more diverse motion-annotated datasets to strengthen both fine-grained moving-object discovery and motion-state prediction. Second, the proposer and propagator could be merged into a single end-to-end trainable framework, allowing the temporal consistency signal to improve mask quality and yield more accurate motion-state predictions over long videos.

Broader impact. Gmos enables real-time identification of moving objects directly from RGB video, supporting safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving, ecological and biomedical monitoring, public-safety surveillance, and dynamic 3D/4D scene reconstruction for robotics and AR/VR. Operating without pre-computed flow or trajectories also lowers the compute footprint of motion-aware perception. We release Gmos-2K and the MOS-I protocol for reproducible research. As with any video-segmentation system, Gmos could be misused in surveillance contexts that raise privacy concerns, particularly when combined with identity-recognition tools. We encourage downstream users to comply with data-protection regulations and obtain appropriate consent.
